summary: Notes by R. W. Watson on a Network Working Group meeting in Urbana, Illinois, 17 February 1971. It was updated by RFC 108 and RFC 123.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 101 is the written record of a three-day meeting of the Network Working Group in Urbana, Illinois, in February 1971. It matters because it shows the network's sites reporting their progress and dividing up the work of writing the protocols.

questions: what was decided at the february 1971 nwg meeting
what was the logger protocol in 1971
which arpanet sites reported status in 1971
subtitle: Richard Watson's notes on the February 1971 Network Working Group meeting, from site reports to the first committees.

tldr.problem: In early 1971 the sites joining the ARPANET needed to compare progress, settle an interim logger protocol and decide who would work on the open problems.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Working Group met in Urbana, Illinois, heard status reports from each site, adopted the logger protocol of RFC 66 with a correction, and formed committees on host-host, typewriter connection and socket number structure.
tldr.outcome: RFC 101 records what was said and decided. It is a meeting record rather than a specification, and it was later updated by RFC 108 and RFC 123.

sections.title: The Urbana Meeting
sections.content:
This RFC, by Richard W. Watson of SRI-ARC, records the Network Working Group meeting held in Urbana, Illinois, from Wednesday evening, February 17, to Friday, February 19, 1971. Mike Sher opened by welcoming the group and noting that ILLIAC IV was expected to be running that summer, and Steve Crocker then asked for the topics to be discussed.

Attendees described their experience of using the network. John Melvin summarized SRI's use of the Utah PDP-10 to help move SRI from an XDS 940 to a PDP-10: the work started on the network in June 1970, round trip character delays of 4 seconds were not uncommon, and at times there were delays of 8 or 10 minutes. Jim White reported that UCSB and RAND had begun to experiment with the network, that the UCSB NCP had been up during the day for the last 3 or 4 weeks, and that it is about 39K bytes and runs in a 60K byte partition. Observers from the Canadian government and from IBM also spoke.
sections.plainLanguage: People from many research sites met for three days. They compared notes on how well their computers worked over the network.

sections.title: Site Status Reports
sections.content:
On Thursday morning each site reported on its status. BBN reported that there are 15 IMPs connected to the network, described work on a 316 version of the IMP and on a Terminal Interface Processor (TIMP) that can handle up to 64 variable speed terminals, and emphasized three products: a 516 IMP, a 316 IMP and a 316 TIMP. The 316 IMP is less expensive than the 516 IMP and can connect to one host.

Other sites gave expected dates: SDC expected its NCP up in 4 to 6 weeks, Case Western Reserve in two to three months, Harvard in one to two months, SRI-ARC in three or four weeks, MIT's Multics offering regular service in three or four months, and UCLA expecting to be up by March 1 with NCP, logger and typewriter connection program. Alex McKenzie of BBN prepared a status form that representatives filled in that evening, and BBN and the NIC were to prepare a procedure for keeping the information up to date.
sections.plainLanguage: Each team said how close it was to getting its computer ready for the network, and a form was filled in so the status could stay current.

sections.title: Protocol Decisions and Committees
sections.content:
Tom Skinner of Multics opened the logger protocol discussion, saying an interim protocol was wanted so use of the network could get started. After comparing the logger protocol of RFC 80 with that of RFC 66, the group adopted the protocol of RFC 66 with the correction that allocate commands are to be issued after the connection was established. Initial communication to the logger is to be in 7-bit ASCII in an 8-bit field, and it was decided that the eighth bit should be a 0.

Steve Crocker then listed known host-host protocol problems: echo, message type, interrupts, marking and padding, and half duplex versus full duplex while establishing a socket. A committee chaired by S. Crocker was appointed to consider them. A committee chaired by Tom O'Sullivan took up the typewriter connection protocol, covering character set, end of line, interrupts, message format and duplex, and a committee chaired by J. Heafner was to write up the issues behind socket number structure proposals. Link number 223 was first assigned to UCLA for measurement experiments, then found to be already assigned, so link 191 was chosen instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The group picked one set of rules for logging in, then formed small committees, each responsible for fixing one kind of problem.

sections.title: The NIC and Next Steps
sections.content:
Dick Watson reviewed the Network Information Center (NIC) at SRI, which works through a Station Agent and a Network Liaison person at each site. Planned online services included access to a typewriter version of the On-Line System (NLS), a message service and the NIC catalog. The group discussed privacy when conversations are filed, microfilm for storing an expanded collection of documents, file transfer by name between hosts, and accounting.

The final question was the frequency and utility of the NWG meetings. The general consensus was that the meeting had been useful but that more preparation on specific topics should be done ahead of time. People who wanted to bring up topics were asked to distribute position or introductory papers about a month ahead of the next meeting, if possible.
sections.plainLanguage: One office kept the papers and notes for everyone. At the end the group agreed that the next meeting would go better if people prepared in advance.
